fieldChanges.before: The birthdays in Google Calendar are not ordinary events. They come from Google Contacts, so the fix for a wrong date lives there, and one calendar setting can remove them all at once. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, explains which control to use.
fieldChanges.after: A birthday on Google Calendar can be manually created or linked to Google Contacts. Find the source and Google account before changing a date or removing a duplicate-looking row. before.q: I deleted a birthday from Calendar. Is it gone from my contact?
before.a: No. Google says deleting a birthday from Calendar does not affect what is stored in Google Contacts.

before.q: How do I stop seeing birthdays without losing them?
before.a: Uncheck the Birthdays calendar in the calendar list. Turning off Sync from Contacts deletes them.

after.q: I deleted a birthday from Calendar. Is it gone from my contact?
after.a: No. Google says deleting a birthday from Calendar does not affect what is stored in Google Contacts.

after.q: How do I stop seeing birthdays without losing them?
after.a: Uncheck the Birthdays calendar in the list to hide its manual and imported entries. Turning off Sync from Contacts instead removes synced Calendar entries and their changes;the underlying contact information remains in Contacts.

For multiple Google accounts, Google documents Settings > Birthdays > Sync from Contacts, with a checkbox beside each account. Inspect which accounts contribute birthdays before changing anything. If you only want a temporary uncluttered view, unchecking the Birthdays calendar hides both manual and imported birthdays without using those account-sync removal controls.

before: Google states that by default only you can find events from Gmail, even if you share your calendar. You can change this under Settings, Google Workspace smart features, Show events from Gmail, Privacy of email events, choosing Calendar default, Private or Only me, and then whether to apply it to new events or all events.

Google’s definitions: Calendar default shows the event name and time to anyone who can access your calendar; Private shows them to you and specific people who can make changes to your calendar; Only me keeps them to you. For a single event you can also open it, choose Edit event and set Default visibility, Public or Private; Google says Public exposes it to anyone who finds a publicly shared calendar.
after: Google states that by default only you can find events from Gmail, even if you share your calendar. You can change this under Settings, Google Workspace smart features, Show events from Gmail, Privacy of email events, choosing Calendar default, Private or Only me, and then whether to apply it to new events or all events.

Google’s Gmail-specific help describes Calendar default as showing name and time to calendar viewers, and Private as including people allowed to edit. The generic calendar-permission documentation describes more detailed viewer/editor levels. These sources do not give a fully explicit matrix for every combination. Do not infer exactly what a particular free/busy viewer or restricted editor receives without checking a harmless example from that account.

Only me is different from Private. Private can still expose an event to permitted editors, while the Gmail help describes Only me as user-only. Anyone using your signed-in Google account on a device can still see its events;the setting is not a way to hide information from someone with access to that same account. A single Gmail-derived event also has documented Default visibility, Public and Private choices;review their actual audience before changing one.

fieldChanges.after: A fictional user shares a calendar with a partner at See event details and a manager at free/busy. A train reservation and a sensitive appointment are added from Gmail. The user checks that the global Gmail setting remains Only me instead of assuming either recipient can or cannot see a later widened setting.

fieldChanges.before: With Only me (Google’s default behaviour), neither person sees them. The user wants the partner to see travel, so they switch Privacy of email events to Calendar default and apply it to new events only. The appointment, which arrived earlier, stays private. Google’s definition of Calendar default says the name and time are visible to anyone who can access the calendar, so before choosing it the user also considers the manager, who has free/busy access, and is comfortable with a train time and title being seen.
fieldChanges.after: Before sharing travel through Calendar, the user inspects the documented per-event visibility options and verifies a harmless record with the intended recipient. They do not widen all future Gmail events merely to share one train journey. If the audience cannot be established confidently, they send the necessary travel details directly through an appropriate channel and leave sensitive bookings user-only.

fieldChanges.before: Check: ask the partner whether the next train booking appears, and confirm the earlier appointment still does not.
fieldChanges.after: Changing a global setting can apply to new events or all events, so read that choice explicitly. Verify the earlier sensitive appointment separately after any change. This example does not claim the free/busy manager sees a particular title, or that Private is equivalent to Only me.

fieldChanges.before: If reminders you set on Keep notes now look different, they have probably become tasks. Google’s migration kept most of the data but changed a few behaviours that are easy to miss. Arte Soft, the developer of Cloud Calendars, summarises what Google documents.
fieldChanges.after: Google announced that Keep reminders would move to Tasks in the second half of 2025. Its help page still uses that dated future-tense wording, so it does not prove that every account has completed migration. Use the documented markers and behavior below to check your actual reminders. Arte Soft develops Cloud Calendars.

fieldChanges.before: What Google says happened
fieldChanges.after: Check the account rather than assume the rollout state

fieldChanges.before: Google’s page states that Keep reminders migrate to Google Tasks and that new reminders are saved as tasks; it dates the migration to the second half of 2025. Migrated reminders move with the same data and stay visible on the Keep note and in Tasks.
fieldChanges.after: Google’s page describes new Keep reminders being saved as Tasks and existing reminders moving with their data. It names the second half of 2025 as the migration period but still phrases that announcement in future tense. Treat the behaviors below as Google’s documented migration design, not a fresh measurement that every current account has finished it.

before: Location-based reminders: Google says you can no longer create or receive them; existing location data can be reviewed in the task description. If you relied on “remind me when I get to the shop”, you now need a time instead.

Long titles are shortened. Repeating reminders are capped: Google says the maximum interval for repeating tasks in Calendar is 1,000 days, weeks, months or years, and longer intervals are adjusted down. Dates beyond the year 3000 are adjusted to 2900.
after: Location-based reminders: Google says you can no longer create or receive them; existing location data can be reviewed in the task description. If you relied on “remind me when I get to the shop”, you now need a time instead.

Long titles are shortened. Repeating reminders are capped: Google says the maximum interval for repeating tasks in Calendar is 1,000 days, weeks, months or years, and longer intervals are adjusted down. Dates beyond the year 3000 are adjusted to 2900.

Notification and title changes deserve their own check. Google says reminder notifications no longer come from Keep;install Calendar or Tasks on the mobile device and allow its notifications. To rename the reminder, use Tasks or Calendar:changing only the Keep note’s title does not update the reminder title. The From Keep link can return you to the original note.

fieldChanges.before: Google says non-repeating reminders older than one year go to a list called “Old Google Keep Reminders”. If an account had more than 100,000 tasks, the oldest reminders do not migrate. And for Workspace accounts where the Tasks service is turned off, data does not migrate; that is an administrator setting, not something you can fix yourself.
fieldChanges.after: Google gives a 100,000-task limit and says that if the number of Keep reminders exceeds that limit, the oldest reminders do not migrate. Non-repeating reminders older than a year go to Old Google Keep Reminders. For work or school accounts, the Tasks service must be enabled;Google also excludes reminders for suspended Workspace licenses. Check the actual account and ask the administrator rather than infer a migration result from a missing row.

fieldChanges.before: A fictional user had three Keep reminders: renew a passport (dated, one-off, two years old), water plants (repeating every 3 days) and buy stamps (location: post office).
fieldChanges.after: For an illustration conditional on migration, a user compares three Keep reminders:an old one-off passport reminder, a plant reminder every 3 days and a former post-office location reminder. They first look for From Keep and compare the original notes, without assuming the dated rollout notice proves what happened in their account.

fieldChanges.before: In Tasks, the passport reminder is in “Old Google Keep Reminders” because it is older than a year and does not repeat. The plant reminder repeats as before. The stamps reminder has no location trigger; its description shows the location, so the user gives it a date and time.
fieldChanges.after: The documented outcomes would put the non-repeating reminder older than a year in Old Google Keep Reminders, retain an ordinary three-day interval within the stated limit, and keep former location data in the task description without a location trigger. The user can add a time if a scheduled reminder fits the real need. They also check Calendar or Tasks notification permission and avoid renaming only the Keep note when the reminder title needs changing.

before: Google says that when you complete it, the task is crossed out and the next instance appears in your task list on the date specified. The page does not say whether completing early or late moves the next date, so check the next occurrence after completing one.
after: Google says that when you complete it, the task is crossed out and the next instance appears in your task list on the date specified. The page does not say whether completing early or late moves the next date, so check the next occurrence after completing one.

Google also says only a limited number of future recurring tasks appear on the Calendar grid at once;new ones become visible as time passes. A partial future list alone does not establish that the series has stopped.

fieldChanges.before: Later they want the task on a shared list. Google says recurring tasks can’t be moved to other lists and shared tasks can’t repeat, so instead of moving it they keep it personal and add a calendar event for the household.
fieldChanges.after: Later they want to share the recurring responsibility with others. Google says shared tasks cannot repeat and a recurring task cannot move to another list. They keep the personal task and coordinate the household separately, for example with an appropriately shared calendar event. Google’s explicit data-loss warning is under Clear your Calendar app data:that action can erase unsynced event information absent from the web calendar. It is not a statement that merely checking connectivity or visibility deletes events. Preserve unsynced details before considering storage clearing, which Google reserves for when other steps fail.

fieldChanges.before: In Android settings, make sure account sync is on for Calendar. In the Calendar app’s settings for the specific calendar, make sure Sync is on at the top of the page. Both must be on; one does not imply the other.
fieldChanges.after: In Android’s account settings, check that Calendar account sync is enabled. Inside Google Calendar, the separate Sync switch is documented for calendars the user created, not the primary calendar, which normally appears as Events. Do not assume every primary or received calendar has an identical per-calendar switch. Check the setting only where the actual calendar supports it.

fieldChanges.before: A fictional user created “Car service, Thu 08:30” on their phone, but their partner cannot see it on the shared calendar. On a computer, the event is not there. The user writes down the details first.
fieldChanges.after: A fictional user created Car service on Thursday at 08:30 in Home maintenance, a secondary Google calendar they created and shared with a partner. The event is absent from the web calendar, so they preserve its details before considering any destructive operation.

fieldChanges.before: They check: Wi-Fi on; app up to date; the shared calendar is ticked; the event was saved to “Family”, which belongs to their Google account. Android account sync for Calendar is on, but Sync for the Family calendar in the app is off. Turning it on and tapping Refresh uploads the event; it appears on the web a moment later.
fieldChanges.after: They check connectivity, the account, the selected calendar and account-level Calendar sync. For this created secondary calendar, they also find its Sync setting off. They enable it, refresh and allow time for the event to appear, as Google warns synchronization can take time. A possible successful result is the same appointment appearing on the web and then for the partner;it is verified rather than promised immediately.

fieldChanges.after: Google says anyone with Make changes and manage sharing permission receives an email when a user under 13 shares the family calendar, makes it public or changes member permissions. That audience is permission-based;do not assume it is exactly the guardians or that every guardian necessarily receives the notice.

fieldChanges.before: A fictional family of four uses Family for school runs and holidays. The eldest moves out and leaves the family group, losing access. They still want holiday dates, so a parent shares the calendar with them by name at See all event details. Because any member can manage sharing, the parents agree that only they will change who has access.
fieldChanges.after: A fictional family of four uses Family for school runs and holidays. The eldest leaves the family group and loses that membership-based access. If the family wants to provide selected continuing access, they inspect the named sharing grant deliberately. Google warns non-family members can edit by default, so a parent should choose and verify the intended view-only permission, not assume that sending another invitation is automatically read-only. An agreement that only parents change sharing is a household rule;it does not technically remove other members’ existing capabilities.

fieldChanges.before: Later the family group is dissolved. The calendar remains, so the owner decides whether to keep it as an ordinary shared calendar or delete it.
fieldChanges.after: If the family group is later deleted, the calendar and events are not automatically deleted according to Google. The owner then inspects the remaining ownership and recipients before deciding whether to retain or delete it. Group deletion is not proof the remaining calendar has exactly the audience the family wants.

before: Click Settings menu, then Print. On the preview page you can change font size, orientation (Landscape or Portrait), deselect Show weekends and choose a colour style. You can also select Print descriptions and Print your response. Google notes that when space is available, event locations or rooms are shown too.
Leave descriptions off for anything handed to others; notes often hold phone numbers, links or private context.
after: Click Settings menu > Print to inspect the preview. Google documents font, orientation, weekends and colour options. For the specific Print descriptions and Print your response controls, its instructions first switch the view to Schedule, then open Print. Do not assume those detail controls appear in every grid view. Event locations or rooms may also appear when space permits.
Leave descriptions off for anything handed to others; notes often hold phone numbers, links or private context.

Changing font size can improve readability, but Google says it does not change the number of days on the page. Choose the view and period separately, then inspect the actual preview rather than infer a new date range from larger text.

fieldChanges.before: For a babysitter, they print the coming Week view with Print descriptions on, so pickup notes appear, but only after checking those descriptions contain nothing beyond what the babysitter needs.
fieldChanges.after: For a babysitter who needs pickup notes, the parent switches to Schedule, opens Print and chooses Print descriptions only after reviewing the notes.
